n: Job’s final oath of innocence begins. He made a solemn promise with his eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman. His integrity reached even his thoughts.

f.w: I made a covenant with mine eyes

f.g: A young woman, a virgin.

n: What reward from God above would come to someone who broke such a promise?

f.g: Allotted share or reward.

n: Disaster is for the wicked, and calamity for evildoers — Job knows the moral law and has lived by it.

f.g: Disaster, misfortune.

n: God sees all his ways and counts every step, so Job’s conduct is open before him.
Job begins a series of “if… then” oaths. If he has lived falsely or hurried toward deceit…

f.g: Falsehood, emptiness.

n: …let God weigh him on honest scales and he will see Job’s integrity.
If he has strayed from the right path, let his heart follow his eyes into sin, or let anything wrong stick to his hands…

f.w: mine heart walked after mine eyes

f.g: A stain or defect — guilt.

n: …then let others eat what he plants and let his crops be uprooted.

f.w: let me sow, and let another eat

n: If he has been seduced by another man’s wife or lurked at his neighbor’s door…

f.w: laid wait at my neighbour's door

n: …then let his own wife serve another man. Job uses a harsh ancient curse to show how serious adultery is.

f.g: Grind grain as another man’s servant — likely also a euphemism for sexual relations.

n: Adultery is a shameful crime that deserves judgment by the courts.

f.g: Shameful, wicked.

f.w: iniquity to be punished by the judges

n: It is a fire that burns all the way to destruction and would uproot everything he has.
If he ever brushed aside the complaint of a servant who had a grievance against him…

f.w: despise the cause of my manservant
f.g: Refused to give a servant a fair hearing.

n: …what could he say when God rose up to judge him?

f.g: When God comes to inspect or judge.

n: A remarkable statement of equality: the same God who made Job in the womb made his servants too. They are equals before God.

f.w: did not one fashion us in the womb?

n: If he denied the poor what they needed or let a widow’s eyes grow dim with despair…

f.w: caused the eyes of the widow to fail
f.g: Made her lose hope while waiting for help.

n: …or ate his bread alone without sharing it with the orphan…
(In fact, from his youth he raised the orphan like a father and guided the widow all his life.)

f.g: The widow — Job cared for her from his earliest days.

n: If he ever saw someone dying for lack of clothes, or a poor person with nothing to cover himself…
…and that person didn’t bless him for being warmed by wool from his sheep…

f.g: Here the body itself, warmed by his clothing gift.
Wool.

n: If he raised a fist against an orphan because he knew the court at the gate would side with him…

f.g: Support in the town court, where Job had great influence.

n: …then let his arm fall from his shoulder and break at the joint. The punishment fits the misused arm.

f.g: The shoulder.

n: Fear of God’s judgment and awe at his majesty kept Job from such deeds.

f.g: His majesty, exaltedness.

n: If he had trusted in gold or called fine gold his security…
…or rejoiced simply because he had become wealthy…
…or looked at the shining sun or the bright moon as gods to be worshipped…
…and his heart was secretly drawn, or he blew a kiss of worship toward them…

f.w: my mouth hath kissed my hand
f.g: An ancient gesture of worship toward the heavenly bodies.

n: …that would be a crime deserving judgment, for he would have betrayed the God above.

f.w: denied the God that is above

n: Job did not gloat over the downfall of his enemy or celebrate when trouble struck him.

f.w: rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me

n: He never let his mouth sin by calling down a curse on his enemy’s life.

f.w: wishing a curse to his soul

n: His household servants could testify that everyone was fed at Job’s table.

f.w: Oh that we had of his flesh!
f.g: Better “Who has not been filled with his meat?” — no one went hungry.

n: No traveler had to sleep in the street, for Job opened his doors to strangers — the duty of hospitality.

f.w: I opened my doors to the traveller

n: Job did not hide his sins as Adam did in the garden, or bury his guilt in his heart.

f.g: Or “as men do” — the Hebrew adam can mean either.

n: He never kept quiet or stayed indoors out of fear of the crowd or the scorn of powerful families. He lived openly.

f.g: Disapproval of the leading clans.

n: Job cries for a hearing and signs his statement: let the Almighty answer him! Let his accuser write out the charges.

f.g: Literally “here is my mark” — like a signature on a legal document.

f.w: mine adversary had written a book
f.g: If only my opponent would put the charges in writing.

n: He would wear the written charge proudly on his shoulder like a badge, or as a crown, confident it would clear him.

f.g: He would display it openly, sure of his innocence.

n: He would account to God for every step, approaching him like a prince — not a cringing criminal.

f.w: as a prince would I go near unto him

n: A final oath: if his land has cried out against him and its furrows wept…

f.w: If my land cry against me

n: …if he ate its produce without paying the workers, or broke the hearts of its owners…

f.g: Without paying fair wages.

n: …let thorns and weeds grow instead of grain. Job rests his case — he has nothing more to say.

f.g: A foul-smelling weed.

f.w: The words of Job are ended
f.g: Job will speak again only briefly to the Lord (40:3-5; 42:1-6).
